tagline.text: A seaside village on Mindoro's north coast that serves as the base for Puerto Galera divers

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000–6,000 (excluding accommodation, per day including 1–2 fun dives)

children.text: Sabang Beach is a narrow beachfront village on the northern peninsula of Puerto Galera and the area's biggest diving base, where wreck and coral garden dives start right in front of the beach. It takes about four hours from Manila by bus and boat, so a weekend trip is possible, and after dark the bars and restaurants turn the strip into a loud, lively night scene.
Sabang is a village in the municipality of Puerto Galera, Oriental Mindoro, on a northern peninsula about
5km

from Puerto Galera town. More dive centers are packed along this one beach than anywhere else nearby, so it is known as the area's diving hub. Several sites are only a few minutes by boat from the beachfront, so you can start diving without a long boat ride. One source says that around 30 years ago it was still a sleepy fishing village.

Puerto Galera lies close to the Verde Island Passage, at the heart of the Coral Triangle, and is known for its rich marine biodiversity. From Sabang you can choose coral gardens, wrecks, macro (small-critter) sites and current-driven drift dives, all from one village. Centers offer everything from beginner discovery dives and certification courses to technical diving courses, and several training agencies, including PADI and SSI, are represented.

The village looks very different by day and by night. During the day it buzzes with divers carrying gear onto bangkas, and after dark the bars, restaurants and karaoke places along the beach road light up. With 24-hour bars and clubs, it is a noisy strip that may not suit travelers who want a quiet getaway. Guides disagree about its nightlife, and many advise families to choose one of the quieter beaches nearby.

The beach itself is not a long, broad resort beach. Dive resorts, guesthouses and restaurants crowd a narrow strip of sand, and the focus is on diving and exploring the village rather than swimming. If you want a calmer beach, Big La Laguna and Small La Laguna are said to be about
15 minutes
away on foot to the west. Accommodation around Sabang ranges from budget rooms to mid-range resorts, so both backpackers and divers come here.
Three wrecks sunk in front of the beach are Sabang's signature dive sites. Two wooden hulls and a steel Chinese fishing-boat-type hull sunk in 1993 rest on a sandy bottom at roughly
. Batfish and scorpionfish are often seen, and only experienced divers can penetrate the steel wreck. It is also a popular night dive.

blocks.title: Coral Gardens and Macro Life Close to the Beach

children.text: You don't have to go far to see coral and seagrass beds right in front of the beach. Giant Clams is a protected, current-free site with a maximum depth of about
, and Monkey Beach is known as a sloping macro site. More than 180 species of nudibranchs have reportedly been recorded around Puerto Galera.

blocks.title: Hole in the Wall and the Canyons

children.text: Hole in the Wall is a swim-through under a rock arch at about
, and the Canyons is a drift dive in strong current at about
. The Canyons is for experienced divers and the current is often strong, so follow your local dive center's guidance.
First-time divers can join a discovery dive. One source lists a discovery dive at about
and an Open Water certification course at about
. Prices and schedules differ by center, so it is worth comparing several.

After sunset the beach road fills with bars and restaurants. Names such as Big Apple and The Venue often come up in guides, and some places combine karaoke with pool tables. The noise runs late into the night, so check whether your room faces the beach or sits farther back.

blocks.title: A Walk to the La Laguna Beaches

children.text: Big La Laguna is said to be about
15 minutes
on foot from the west end of Sabang. Many reviews call it quieter and cleaner than Sabang, which makes it a good place to rest on a non-diving day.

blocks.title: Marine Life of the Verde Island Passage

children.text: The Puerto Galera area is described as the center of the Coral Triangle. One source claims the nearby Verde Island Passage holds a large share of the world's known shore fish species, though the figures differ between sources. Some accounts also say protected species such as sea turtles and giant clams live here.
Take a bus from Manila toward Batangas Port. It takes about
2.5–3 hours
; check before leaving that the bus goes all the way to the Batangas pier.
At Batangas Port, board a fast craft or RoRo ferry to Puerto Galera (Balatero Port). The crossing takes about
1–1.5 hours
From Balatero Port, take a tricycle to Sabang and drop your bags at your accommodation. Sources list the tricycle fare from the port to Sabang at about
Do an afternoon dive at the Sabang Wrecks. If you are already certified, it is a good idea to get one dive in on arrival day.
Have dinner at a restaurant on the beach road and stroll the night strip. Night dives are booked separately through the dive center.
Do a morning dive at Monkey Beach or Giant Clams. After lunch, pack up and head back.
The last boat time varies by season, so check the boat schedule for your return day in advance.
Have breakfast at your lodging, then walk Sabang Beach and watch divers boarding bangkas and the village coming to life.
Walk west to Big La Laguna beach, about
15 minutes
away. Swim and relax on the quieter beach.
Eat lunch at one of the restaurants on the Sabang beach road.
Rent a bangka for snorkeling or try a discovery dive. Ask first what the price includes, such as equipment and a safety briefing.
Snorkeling bangka and discovery dive prices differ by center, so compare on site before you decide.

Fares and schedules differ widely between sources and change with the season. Check the latest information at the port ticket counter before you leave.
A tricycle is the most common way from the port to Sabang, which is listed as about
10 km
away. Sources list the fare at about

Jeepneys also run between Puerto Galera town and Sabang.
Higher-end resorts sometimes pick up guests at the port and bring them straight to Sabang.
You can walk the whole Sabang beach road.
Motorbikes are listed at under
a day, but this varies by season and shop. Wear a helmet and check road conditions.
The La Laguna beaches are about
15 minutes
away on foot.

You can dive year-round, but weather and sea conditions change with the season. One dive guide treats November–May as the dry season and says the sea is calmest in March–May. Monthly climate data for the same area show January–April as the driest months, so sources divide the seasons slightly differently.
June–October is the rainy and typhoon season, with frequent rain and sometimes rough seas, although some accounts say visibility can improve then. Visibility is usually listed at about
, over 30 m on good days, and around
at macro sites.
Water temperature is listed at about
in March–October and about

in December–February. A 3 mm wetsuit is enough for most of the year, and some operators recommend a thicker one in December–February. Rooms and boat seats fill up fast in peak season and on holidays, so book ahead.

Lodging splits into beachfront resorts, guesthouses set back from the beach, and cheap rooms at the west end. One source says rooms at the west-end resorts start at a few hundred pesos without air conditioning. Resorts run by dive centers are convenient to book together with diving packages. Because of the noise, if you want a room away from the night strip, look at places away from the beach or toward La Laguna.

Restaurants along the beach road serve Filipino home cooking, grilled seafood and Western food. A 2026 visitor review, however, rates Sabang's hotels and restaurants as poor value for the price, so opinions are mixed. One source mentions beer at around one US dollar a bottle, and prices vary by shop.
Puerto Galera town has more markets and restaurants and prices are a little lower. Bring water and light snacks to eat between dives.
Compare at least two or three dive centers on price, equipment condition and instructor credentials before you choose.
If you bring your dive certification card, you can go straight in at the fun dive rate; bring your logbook too.
If you are flying out after diving, respect the no-fly time and leave plenty of margin for your last day's dives.
If you lack experience, do not enter strong-current sites such as the Canyons; follow the dive center's guidance.
At the port, ignore touts and buy your tickets directly at the ticket counter.
Boat schedules and fares change with season and operator, so check before booking.
Bring plenty of pesos in cash. Some shops on the beach road may not accept cards.
The environmental and terminal fees are paid separately at the port, so have small change ready.
Many guides describe Sabang as loud at night, with some areas having a seedy feel. Keep a close eye on your belongings and drinks, and stay with your group late at night.
Overcharging and touting can happen on the night strip, so confirm prices before you pay.
Currents and visibility change from day to day. Don't push yourself on days when you don't feel well.
In the rainy and typhoon season, boats can be cancelled or rescheduled, so leave some slack in your return plans.
If you rent a motorbike, check the insurance and its condition, and avoid riding at night.
Do not touch or step on coral and marine life, and keep your distance.
The resort town that Sabang belongs to, with its town center, White Beach and a market; you can get there from Sabang by tricycle.
A wider beach than Sabang where swimmers gather; it has a very different character from Sabang.
An island in the strait on the Batangas side, known for diving and island tours.
A quiet beach about
15 minutes
on foot west of Sabang, described as calmer than Sabang.
